ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure: 15 minutes ago stung by a wasp while gardening.
- Symptom timeline and progression: Immediate onset of “shallow” breathing and chest tightness; tingling sensation of lips; blotchy rash noted on body; no throat-closing sensation reported.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: Denied.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: Not reported.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Not reported.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: None reported.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: Not reported.  
  • Dyspnea: Yes—described as shallow breathing and chest tightness.  
  • Swelling distribution: Tingling in lips; patient unsure of visible swelling.  
  • Ear/neck symptoms: None acutely; history of aerosinusitis when flying.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments: No prior similar reactions; no previous ED visits or adrenaline injections for allergies.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug allergy: Penicillin (reaction details not provided).  
  • Current regular medications: None documented.  
  • PRN medication in home: Oral antihistamine (exact name/dose/route/frequency not documented) used previously for flying-related ear issues; not yet taken today.
- Social context: Wife present in the home and able to assist.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: Not directly observed; patient reports lip tingling without confirmed swelling.
- Airway/breathing: Patient reports shallow breathing and chest tightness; no report of stridor.
- Mental status/associated features: Appears alert and oriented via conversation.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person: Wife present and calling emergency services.

Assessment:
- Suspected evolving systemic allergic reaction with early airway/respiratory involvement after wasp sting; risk of progression to anaphylaxis. Justified by recent insect sting trigger, rapid onset lip tingling, dyspnea, chest tightness, and cutaneous rash.

Plan:
- Advised immediate activation of emergency services (ambulance) rather than private transport.
- Instructed wife to administer available oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.
- Recommended hospital evaluation for possible anaphylaxis management (airway support, epinephrine, monitoring).
- Escalation/red-flag advice: Worsening breathing difficulty, throat tightness, voice change, stridor, facial/tongue swelling, dizziness, or collapse—call EMS immediately if not already en route.
- Follow-up: ED care today; subsequent referral to allergy/ENT clinic for definitive assessment and consideration of carry epinephrine auto-injector and sting avoidance education once acute episode resolved.
- Patient advised to remain accompanied until definitive care obtained.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: vital signs, direct visualization of airway/oral cavity, documentation of antihistamine type/dose, information on availability of epinephrine auto-injector, full drug/allergy list, prior anaphylaxis management plan.  
● Internal conflicts: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional minor inaudible segments without loss of clinically relevant data.
